extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of classical mathematics/geometry and history of science
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted sections from Archimedes covering the Sand-Reckoner number scheme, the Quadrature of the Parabola (propositions and lemmas about parabolic segments), and Book I of On Floating Bodies (postulate and first propositions). Includes definitions, theorems, constructions and physical postulates for fluids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scheme of orders and periods of numbers (Sand‑Reckoner)
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional names for numbers up to a myriad (10,000) are extended by treating 100,000,000 as a unit of higher orders and forming successive 'orders' and 'periods' (first period: numbers 1 to 10^8; second period: P to 10^8 P; ... up to the 100,000,000th order/period), producing enormously large named numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains how to build hierarchical number-naming by taking 100,000,000 as the unit of the next order and iterating; gives index-based exposition and shows the prodigious scale (e.g., last number of first period would be represented by 1 followed by 800,000,000 ciphers). Includes examples and index notation to make the scheme clearer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Octads and placement of geometric progression terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the geometric progression 1, 10, 10^2, 10^3, ... ; 'octads' (blocks of 8 terms) are placed under successive orders: first octad 1..10^7 under first order, second octad under second order, etc., enabling placement of any number of octads within the orders scheme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to map powers of ten into the orders/periods scheme; allows reasoning about terms of wide-ranging magnitude when applying the number scheme to physical estimations (e.g., grains of sand).

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem on products in continued proportion (geometric progression)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a series is in continued proportion with A1=1, A2=10 (i.e., geometric progression 1,10,10^2,...), then for any two terms Am, An their product Am * An is also a term of the same series and lies at a position related to the distances of Am and An from the first term; the positional index of the product differs by one less than the sum of the respective term-distances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives a constructive index-based reasoning: choose the term at equal term-distance etc., and uses proportionality of equally-distant terms in continued proportion to prove the index-addition property. Used later in counting large numbers of grains by composing powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumptions for physical estimation (poppy-seed model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume a poppy-seed contains not more than 10,000 grains and its diameter is not less than 1/4 of a finger-breadth; spheres relate in triplicate ratio of diameters (volume ∝ diameter^3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These physical assumptions are foundational to the calculation estimating the number of grains of sand that would fill spheres of various diameters (up to a model 'universe'). The text multiplies diameters by factors of 100 and uses the triplicate ratio to scale grain counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application: upper bound on grains of sand filling 'universe' sphere
rubrics_metrics.description: Using the diameter estimates and orders/periods scheme, the number of grains of sand that could fill a sphere of diameter less than 10,000,000,000 stadia is shown to be less than 1,000 units of the seventh order (i.e., < 10^51).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combines the poppy-seed assumptions, volume scaling (×10^6 per ×100 diameter), and the number nomenclature to place an upper bound; also extends to sphere of fixed stars via proportionality assumptions attributed to Aristarchus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quadrature program: use of mechanical methods and rigorous geometric proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Archimedes states he first discovered the quadrature of the parabola by means of mechanics and then provided a geometric demonstration, assuming lemmas about making an excess exceed any finite area by repeated doubling (a completeness-type lemma).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains methodological approach: discovery via mechanical reasoning (balancing) followed by geometric proofs; notes the reliance on an assumption/lemma used by earlier geometers (ability to make excess arbitrarily large by addition) which underpins proofs of area ratios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 1 (Parabola: chord parallel to tangent implies equal segments)
rubrics_metrics.description: If from a point P on a parabola a line PV (axis or parallel to axis) is drawn and QQ' is a chord parallel to the tangent at P meeting PV in V, then OV = VQ. Conversely, if QV = VQ' then chord QQ' is parallel to the tangent at P.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives a geometric relation between a chord parallel to a tangent and the intersection point on the diameter/axis; used as a fundamental lemma in coordinate-like manipulations of parabolic segments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 2 (Relations among diameters, chord, tangent intersections)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a chord QQ' parallel to the tangent at P, and a line through P (axis or parallel) meeting QQ' in V and tangent at Q in T, there is a specific proportional relation among segments formed (statement given in the text in geometric proportions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides algebraic/proportional relations between distances obtained from geometric configuration (serves to convert between tangent/chord distances and diameters); used in subsequent coordinate-like derivations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 3 (Pairs of chords parallel to tangent yield proportionalities)
rubrics_metrics.description: If from P a diameter PV is drawn and from two other points Q, Q' chords are drawn parallel to the tangent at P meeting PV in V, V' respectively, then PV : PV' = QV : Q'V'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishes proportional changes along the axis corresponding to chords parallel to one tangent; useful for constructing continued proportional relations in the parabola.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 4 (Change of axes relation / continued proportion identity)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Qq is the base of any parabolic segment with vertex P, and the diameter through a point R meets Qq in O and QP (produced) in F, then OV : VO? = OF : FR (presented as continued proportion relations); PQ, PF, PK are in continued proportion leading to algebraic coordinate relation py = x(2a−x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interprets geometric proportions as an equivalent to changing axes of coordinates (from tangent & diameter to chord & diameter), giving an analytic relation between coordinates; used to derive the parabolic equation in geometric form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 5 (Further proportional relation involving tangent intersection)
rubrics_metrics.description: With Qq base and P vertex and diameter through R meeting Qq in O and tangent at P in E, the relation QO:QOg = ER:RO holds (geometric proportional equality among segments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proves relations by constructing auxiliary points and using doubling arguments; supports the conversion between chord/diameter/tangent distances for later area arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositions 6–7 (Center of gravity of a triangle via lever equilibrium)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a horizontal lever supported at midpoint O, a triangle BCD (right or obtuse at C) suspended appropriately will be in equilibrium when a point-mass P equal to the area (triangle) is hung at A; the midpoint G of a certain segment (constructed) is the centre of gravity of the triangle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses mechanical equilibrium (lever) arguments to identify centers of gravity of plane figures; these balancing arguments are used repeatedly to relate areas to weights, crucial for the mechanical method of quadrature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositions 8–9 (Bounds via balancing trapezia and triangles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a triangle BCD suspended from two points and an area P that balances it when suspended from A, P is less than ABCD but greater than a certain constructed Q; uses center of gravity location to compare areas and deduce inequalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides inequalities comparing the area required for equilibrium and certain subareas (Q), building tools for constructing upper and lower sums approximating parabolic segments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositions 10–11 (Trapezium center of gravity and bounds)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a trapezium CDEF placed with parallel sides vertical and suspended at chosen points, there exists an area P (when suspended from A) that balances it; relationships between AO:OK and trapezium:P give inequality P < trapezium and comparisons with a reference Q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructs the centre of gravity of a trapezium and uses lever proportionality to bound the balancing area; used to compare sums of inscribed trapezia/triangles with the full parabolic segment area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositions 12–13 (Monotone ordering of balancing areas)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the trapezium CDEF is suspended from different points L,H producing areas Q,R respectively and P balances when suspended from A, then P lies between Q and R (i.e., Q < P < R).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows how changing suspension points changes the balancing area monotonically; used to compare approximating pieces in the partitioning of the parabolic segment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositions 14–15 (Partitioning base into equal parts and trapezoidal approximations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide base Qq into equal parts and draw through division points diameters meeting the parabola and tangent, forming sequences of trapezia and triangles; prove inequalities that the area of the parabolic segment is bounded between 3 times certain sums of trapezia (upper/lower bounds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets up the exhaustion method: partition the base, form inscribed trapezia and triangles, and derive inequalities bounding the segment area between sums of simpler shapes; foundational for the exhaustion/limit argument proving the 4/3 ratio.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 16 (Segment area equals one-third of triangle AEqQ)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a parabolic segment with base Qq (q no farther than Q from vertex), the area of the segment equals 1/3 of triangle AEqQ (with A chosen appropriately in the construction); proves by contradiction using submultiples and previously established bounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses the exhaustion bounds from Propositions 14–15 and contradiction by constructing submultiples of a triangle to show the segment cannot be greater or less than the asserted fraction; an intermediate step toward the 4/3 result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 17 (Area of parabolic segment is 4/3 of inscribed triangle)
rubrics_metrics.description: The area of any parabolic segment is four-thirds of the triangle having the same base and equal height (i.e., area(segment) = (4/3)·area(PQq) where PQq is the inscribed triangle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derives from Prop. 16 and geometric relations between the constructed triangles and parallelograms (use of parallels and the property that certain distances double), giving the celebrated quadrature result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 18 (Vertex identification: diameter through mid-point bisects chord)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Qq is base of a segment and V is the midpoint of Qq, the diameter through V meets curve in P, and P is the vertex of the segment (i.e., the greatest perpendicular from curve to base is at P).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses Prop. 1 to show Qq is parallel to tangent at P and then deduces P gives greatest perpendicular; defines vertex and justifies constructions used earlier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 19 (Relation PV = 4·RM in certain bisected chord/distance setup)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given chord Qq bisected in V by diameter PV and RM a diameter bisecting QV in M with RW the ordinate from R to PV, then PV = 4·RM.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses properties of the parabola and proportional relations to obtain scaling relations between distances; applied in later area decompositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 20 (Triangle PQq greater than half the segment)
rubrics_metrics.description: For parabolic segment with base Qq and vertex P, the triangle PQq is greater than half the segment; as corollary, one can inscribe polygons in the segment so that leftover areas are less than any assigned area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides an elementary bound enabling the exhaustion argument (ensuring inscribed polygons can approximate the segment arbitrarily closely).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 21 (Relation of inscribed triangle areas in successive segments)
rubrics_metrics.description: If R is the vertex of the segment cut off by PQ then area relationships hold: A PQq = 8·A PRq (and similar equalities for successive subdivisions), giving a factor-8 relation between certain inscribed triangles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishes recursive geometric relations (each inscribed triangle relates to the next by a factor of 1/8), enabling the geometric series decomposition of the segment area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 22 (Sum of geometric series of areas less than segment)
rubrics_metrics.description: If areas A, B, C, D,... satisfy each is four times the next and A equals the inscribed triangle PQ, then A + B + C + ... < (area of the parabolic segment PQq).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows that the infinite sum of the descending inscribed triangle areas yields an inscribed polygon area strictly less than the full segment; used in exhaustion/comparison arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 23 (Algebraic identity for geometric series of areas)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a series A, B, C, D,... with each term four times the next, shows A + B + C + ... + (last pair) = 4A (algebraic derivation of the geometric series identity used in the proofs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offers the algebraic summation identity (geometric series with ratio 1/4) used to total the infinite series of inscribed triangle areas; supplies the quantitative backbone to deduce factor 4 relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 24 (Full quadrature: parabolic segment equals 4/3 triangle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every segment bounded by a parabola and a chord Qq is equal to four-thirds of the triangle with the same base and equal height. The proof uses the preceding partitioning, inequalities and geometric series identity to rule out the segment being greater or less than 4/3 of the triangle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finalizes the quadrature via exhaustion: assume > or < and derive contradiction using Propositions 14–23; demonstrates equality precisely and gives the canonical quadrature result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postulate 1 (Fluid continuity and pressure direction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume a fluid whose parts lie evenly and continuously: the part which is thrust the less is driven along by that which is thrust the more; each part is thrust by the fluid above it in a perpendicular direction (i.e., pressure acts normal to surfaces).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foundational physical postulate for the On Floating Bodies book; establishes continuity, transmission of pressures, and perpendicularity of thrust — used to reason about equilibrium and motion in fluids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition I (Surface of revolution with circular plane sections is a sphere)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a surface cut by any plane through a certain point always gives a circle whose centre is that point, then the surface is a sphere (i.e., all radii from that fixed point to surface are equal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple geometric criterion to identify a sphere via planar cross-sections; used to argue about shapes of fluid surfaces under gravitational centre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 2 (Fluid surface at rest is spherical with centre at earth's centre)
rubrics_metrics.description: The surface of any fluid at rest is the surface of a sphere whose centre is the same as that of the earth: any plane through earth's centre cuts the fluid surface in a circle centred at earth's centre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction using Postulate 1: unequal radii would cause parts of the fluid to be unequally compressed and therefore set in motion; used to justify that large-scale fluid surfaces conform to spherical equipotential surfaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 3 (Body equal in weight per volume to fluid floats exactly at surface)
rubrics_metrics.description: Solids which, size for size, are of equal weight with a fluid, when let into the fluid, will be immersed so that they neither project above the surface nor sink lower (i.e., they are neutrally buoyant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues by contradiction and pressure comparisons using pyramids and spheres centred at earth's centre; foundational buoyancy principle for neutral equilibrium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 4 (A solid lighter than fluid cannot be completely submerged at rest)
rubrics_metrics.description: A solid lighter than a fluid, if immersed, will not be completely submerged in a state of rest; part must project above the surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction using constructed pyramids and comparison of pressures: complete submersion would create unequal pressures and motion; establishes that lighter solids float partially submerged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 5 (Archimedean principle: weight of displaced fluid equals weight of floating body)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any solid lighter than a fluid will be so far immersed that the weight of the solid equals the weight of the fluid displaced by the immersed portion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructs similar pyramids and compares pressures to deduce equality of weights; this is the classical buoyancy principle used for determining floatation depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 6 (Upthrust equals difference between weight and displaced fluid weight)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a solid lighter than a fluid is forcibly immersed, it is driven upward by a force equal to the difference between its weight and the weight of the fluid displaced (i.e., the net buoyant force equals weight_deficit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument uses adding an auxiliary solid to reach neutral buoyancy and infers the upward force on the original solid equals the added weight; formalizes the buoyant force concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 7 (Heavier solids sink; apparent weight reduced by displaced fluid weight)
rubrics_metrics.description: A solid heavier than a fluid will descend to the bottom; when weighed in the fluid it appears lighter by an amount equal to the weight of the fluid displaced (i.e., apparent weight = true weight − weight of displaced fluid).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First part is intuitive (sinks). The second part is proved by combining a heavier solid with a lighter one chosen so combined they are neutrally buoyant; the downward force causing sinking equals the upward force on the lighter part, giving the reduction in apparent weight. This provides the method underlying Archimedes' use in density determinations (e.g., crown problem).
